meta.titre: Defence Mechanisms of the Body: barriers, blood cells and immunity
meta.sous_theme: Physical and chemical barriers, white blood cells, antibodies and immunity

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Human Biology past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A farmer in a village in the North West Region cuts his foot with a cutlass while weeding. Within minutes the bleeding stops and a scab forms, and a few days later the wound is healed, although the soil is full of microbes. Skin, blood clotting, white blood cells and antibodies all played a part. GCE questions ask you to name the barrier, the cell or the chemical, and to say exactly how it protects the body. This course sorts the defences into groups so that each answer has a clear label.

items: Pathogens are microorganisms, such as bacteria, viruses and fungi, that cause disease.
Blood is made of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
Proteins are made of amino acids, and each protein has a specific shape.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Barriers that keep pathogens out

| Barrier | How it protects |
|---|---|
| Skin | The outer layer is tough, made of dead cells, and forms a physical barrier; oily sebum and sweat make the surface slightly acidic, which discourages microbes |
| Blood clot and scab | Platelets and the protein fibrin seal a cut, so pathogens cannot enter |
| Mucus and cilia | In the nose, trachea and bronchi, mucus traps microbes and dust and cilia sweep it up to be swallowed or coughed out |
| Tears and saliva | They contain lysozyme, an enzyme that breaks down the walls of bacteria |
| Stomach acid | Hydrochloric acid kills many microbes swallowed with food |

### Defence by the blood

- **Phagocytes**, a kind of white blood cell, engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis).
- **Lymphocytes**, another kind of white blood cell, make **antibodies**, which are proteins carried in the plasma. An **antigen** is a foreign substance, usually a protein on the surface of a pathogen. Each antibody fits one antigen. Antibodies make pathogens clump together, neutralise toxins and mark bacteria so that phagocytes can engulf them.
- After an infection, some lymphocytes remain as **memory cells**, so that a second infection by the same pathogen is dealt with faster.
- Red blood cells carry oxygen and have no defence role.

### Immunity

| Type | How it is gained | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Active natural | The body makes its own antibodies after an infection | Recovering from measles |
| Active artificial | A vaccine makes the body produce its own antibodies | Polio vaccine |
| Passive natural | Ready-made antibodies pass from mother to baby | Antibodies through the placenta and in breast milk |
| Passive artificial | Ready-made antibodies are injected | Antivenom after a snake bite |

Active immunity lasts long because memory cells are made; passive immunity is short-lived.

variantes.nom: The role of blood in defence
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks how blood protects the body against infection.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give three roles, each with its cell: platelets and fibrin clot the blood and seal wounds; phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies that act on pathogens. The plasma carries the antibodies around the body.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks how a vaccine prevents a disease.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A vaccine contains a weakened or killed pathogen, or part of it, which carries the antigens. It cannot cause the disease, but the lymphocytes respond by making antibodies and memory cells. If the real pathogen enters later, the memory cells cause a rapid, large antibody response and the person does not fall ill.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question links defence to HIV, antibiotics or wounds.
variantes.contenu_markdown: HIV damages certain lymphocytes, so the body can no longer defend itself well. Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses. A deep wound that breaks the skin lets many pathogens in at once.

sections.enonce_markdown: A farmer cuts his foot with a cutlass and soil bacteria enter the wound. Explain how his body deals with these bacteria. *(6 marks)*

etapes.justification: A good answer starts from the point where the first line of defence is broken.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The skin, a physical barrier, has been cut, so bacteria can enter.

etapes.justification: Blood loss and further entry of microbes must be stopped quickly.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Platelets and fibrin form a clot that dries into a scab.

etapes.justification: Bacteria that have entered must be removed by cells.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Phagocytes engulf and digest the bacteria.

etapes.justification: A specific, stronger defence starts with antigens on the bacteria.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Lymphocytes make antibodies that fit the antigens; antibodies clump the bacteria and mark them for phagocytes.

etapes.justification: They explain the lasting protection after the infection.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Some lymphocytes stay as memory cells, giving a faster response to the same bacteria later.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer.** The cut breaks the skin barrier. Platelets and fibrin form a clot and scab that seals the wound. Phagocytes engulf and digest the bacteria. Lymphocytes produce antibodies that fit the antigens on the bacteria, causing them to clump and making them easier for phagocytes to ingest. Memory cells remain and give a faster response if the same bacteria enter again.

items.pourquoi_faux: Engulfing is done by phagocytes. Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes that attach to antigens.
items.correction_markdown: Phagocytes engulf; antibodies attach to antigens, clump the pathogens and mark them.

items.pourquoi_faux: Red blood cells carry oxygen. White blood cells defend the body.
items.correction_markdown: Phagocytes and lymphocytes are the white blood cells involved in defence.

items.pourquoi_faux: A vaccine contains antigens (a weakened or killed pathogen, or part of one). The body makes its own antibodies in response.
items.correction_markdown: Vaccine: antigens, giving active immunity. Antiserum: ready-made antibodies, giving passive immunity.

items.erreur_markdown: "Antibiotics cure viral infections such as influenza."
items.pourquoi_faux: Antibiotics act on bacteria and do not work on viruses.

items.erreur_markdown: "Mucus kills all microbes that enter the nose."
items.pourquoi_faux: Mucus traps microbes and the cilia move the mucus away; killing is done by other defences, such as stomach acid or phagocytes.
items.correction_markdown: Mucus **traps** microbes and cilia **sweep** them out.

items.enonce_markdown: Name: (a) the enzyme in tears that attacks bacteria; (b) the cells that engulf pathogens; (c) the proteins made by lymphocytes; (d) the acid in the stomach that kills microbes; (e) the structures that sweep mucus out of the trachea.

Classify each of the following as active natural, active artificial, passive natural or passive artificial immunity: (i) a baby receives antibodies from its mother's breast milk; (ii) a child is given the polio vaccine; (iii) a person recovers from measles; (iv) a snake-bite victim is injected with antivenom. Explain why passive immunity does not last as long as active immunity.
items.solution_markdown: (i) **Passive natural**. (ii) **Active artificial**. (iii) **Active natural**. (iv) **Passive artificial**. In passive immunity the body is given ready-made antibodies and does not make its own or form memory cells, so the antibodies are broken down and protection soon fades; active immunity leaves memory cells that can respond again.

items.enonce_markdown: In a trial, a person received a vaccine on day 0. The antibody level rose to 20 units after 14 days. A second dose on day 28 raised the level to 160 units by day 32. (a) How many times higher was the level after the second dose? (b) Compare the time taken to reach the peak after each dose. (c) Explain the difference. (d) Give one reason for giving a second dose.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $\frac{160}{20} = 8$, so **8 times higher**. (b) First dose: 14 days. Second dose: $32 - 28 = 4$ days, so **the response was much faster**. (c) After the first dose, lymphocytes had to start from the beginning; memory cells made then respond quickly and in large numbers to the second dose. (d) A booster dose gives a larger and longer-lasting antibody response, so protection is stronger.

items_markdown: First-line barriers are the skin, blood clots, mucus and cilia, lysozyme in tears and saliva, and stomach acid.
Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes make antibodies, which are proteins that fit specific antigens.
Memory cells give a faster, stronger response the second time, which is the basis of vaccination.
Active immunity (infection or vaccine) is long-lasting; passive immunity (breast milk, antiserum) is ready-made and short-lived.
Antibiotics work on bacteria and not on viruses; HIV damages lymphocytes and weakens defence.
